h: Thieves have stolen more than $100 million in data center freight since June
s: More than $100 million. That's how much data center cargo thieves have taken off U.S. highways since June, NBC News reported on October 26, based on accounts from industry executives, consultants and investigators who advise police. Targets include servers, memory chips, fiber-optic cable, copper wire and data center power and cooling gear. In early June, a trailer with about $13 million in server equipment headed for Fayetteville, Georgia, was among the losses. The method is mostly digital: thieves take over freight broker accounts on load boards, post fake loads, send malware links to carriers that respond, then use those carriers' accounts to bid on real shipments. Some use fake driver's licenses, and in one large theft the tracking signal was spoofed. Scott Cornell, chair of TAPA Americas, told FreightWaves in August that two escorted loads were lost after escorts were deliberately hit, and he tied both to drivers who weren't properly vetted. Why it matters: the weak point is carrier and driver verification, which buyers and logistics teams can check before the load moves.

h: SK hynix says its DRAM and HBM output is effectively sold out through 2029
s: Sold out through 2029. SK hynix said on its third-quarter earnings call on October 28 that, counting long-term agreements and deals under discussion, its DRAM and high-bandwidth memory output for the next three years is effectively spoken for, and it expects memory demand to outrun supply through 2030. The company said customer requests for HBM are more than twice what it can supply, and that long-term agreements already cover more than half its capacity for 2027 and 2028. It also expects PC and phone shipments to fall as memory costs rise.

h: SAP starts sending warehouse tasks straight to robots, and logging what they did
s: A humanoid robot at Arçelik-LG now takes its inbound storage tasks from SAP and records the result there. SAP showed the setup at TechEd on October 27 as part of new physical AI capabilities that send tasks from SAP Extended Warehouse Management to robots and write status and exceptions back. In a proof of concept at Intel's Chengdu site, SAP and Intel say material moves were automated end to end, with shorter transport distances and less manual handling; neither company gave figures.

h: Amazon Business lets buyers ask spend questions in plain language
s: Two years of purchase history and more than 60 reporting fields now sit behind a typed question, according to the National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors' MDM. Amazon Business said on October 27 at its Reshape event in Nashville that its Business Assistant can now answer spend questions, track orders and approvals, and suggest how to allocate payments for U.S. customers, with existing permissions and approval rules left in place. It also launched Value Intelligence, a report that combines savings, efficiency and policy compliance, with methods customers can review and adjust.

h: A robot-run U.S. factory says it builds circuit boards in 4 days, at China prices
s: Four days, not nine. That's the average build-and-ship time CircuitHub says its automated circuit board factory in South Deerfield, Massachusetts, now hits, compared with a typical quick-turn shop in China. The company announced on October 26 that the factory, called the Grid, has reached price parity with similar Chinese shops and is expanding capacity fivefold, with a UK site planned for 2027. Levitating movers carry each board between robots that print solder paste, place parts, solder and inspect, and AI routes every board on its own path, so there are no changeovers between designs. CircuitHub says one unit each of 100 designs runs as easily as 100 units of one design, and that it has shipped more than 2.2 million boards. Why it matters: CircuitHub says 95% of electronics projects involve fewer than 10,000 units, and those small, high-mix orders are where offshore lead time and freight hurt most. Price parity is the company's own claim, so test it with a quote.

h: Oracle launches AI agents that draft allocation plans and hunt maverick spend
s: Twenty-five new agentic applications became available across Oracle's Fusion cloud apps on October 26, and three are aimed at supply chain teams. Oracle says Supply Planning Allocation compares scenarios for splitting scarce materials and capacity across competing demand, Shipment Load Planning looks for load consolidation to cut transport cost, and Procurement Spend flags maverick spend and contract leakage. According to Oracle, each one prepares plans or recommendations that people review and approve.

h: TSMC weighs up to 20% higher prices for AI chip packaging
s: Six to eight months. That's how long equipment lead times for advanced chip packaging have stretched, up from three to six, as TSMC weighs raising prices for its CoWoS packaging by 10% to 20%, Taiwan's Commercial Times reported, citing supply chain sources. CoWoS joins AI processors to high-bandwidth memory in data center accelerators, and demand has spread from GPUs to server CPUs and custom chips. TSMC has not confirmed the plan. TrendForce, citing the Liberty Times, says TSMC has also set wafer price increases of 3% to 6% starting January 2027.

h: GXO takes Digit humanoid robots to two more U.S. warehouses
s: More than 100,000 totes. That's how many Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid has moved at GXO's Flowery Branch, Georgia, warehouse under a robots-as-a-service deal signed in 2024, GXO said on October 26. GXO now plans to put Digit to work on repetitive tote handling at e-commerce sites in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee, starting in early 2027. The companies say Digit has logged more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation across all of its deployments.

h: 83% of supply chain leaders say their people aren't ready to use AI
s: 28% versus 71%. That's the AI project success rate for organizations whose people aren't ready, compared with those whose people are, in The People Paradox in Supply Chain AI Integration, a report the Association for Supply Chain Management (ASCM) and the Digital Supply Chain Institute (DSCI) released October 14. FreightWaves interviewed ASCM CEO Abe Eshkenazi about it on October 23. Of 107 qualified respondents, 83% said their employees are unprepared to use AI well, and 64% of the unprepared group is still stuck in pilots or planning. On a scale from 1 (no AI) to 5 (fully autonomous), adoption across 13 supply chain functions averaged 1.94. Demand planning led at 2.28; reverse logistics was last at 1.59. The top barriers tied at 33% each: missing skills and an unclear business case. Why it matters: involvement drops off below the top. 82% of C-suite respondents lead or scale AI work, but 70% of staff say they're aware of it without being involved. The people who run the process aren't helping shape the tool.

h: AI data center tenants now ask $5 million a day when builds run late
s: $5 million a day, up from $1 million this spring. That's what tenants in new AI data center leases are asking developers to pay when power and buildings aren't ready on time, The Information reported on October 25. Insurance broker Marsh designed a delay-in-delivery policy this spring for the $1 million case, then saw new deals ask for five times that within months. Marsh says contractors and suppliers can be asked to backstop those penalties in their own agreements, and that guarantees now cover equipment lead times and energization dates.

h: AWS says its planning agents now rank exceptions by financial impact
s: Close to 200,000 active SKUs across more than 25 plants: that's the network TE Connectivity's planners triage with Amazon Connect Decisions, which now ranks exceptions by financial impact and suggests order-level fixes, AWS wrote on October 23. The post says constraint-aware supply planning (inventory policies, capacity, supplier lead times) is now generally available. One unnamed manufacturer cut the time to build its 52-week plan by 40% while managing 30% more SKUs, per AWS. These are AWS's own figures; the product launched in April.

h: Dexory's scanning robots now flag open boxes and misaligned pallets
s: Open boxes, goods pulled forward and misaligned pallets are now on the list of rack problems Dexory's autonomous scanning robots can flag, the company announced October 21. Its Storage Health feature added NVIDIA's Cosmos-Reason2-2B model, fine-tuned on Dexory's own warehouse images, as a second check when its existing models aren't confident. Dexory says it tested the 2B and 8B versions and picked the smaller one for accuracy and speed. Robotics 24/7 covered the update October 23.

h: Mexico's customs agency shows a tool that flags undervalued imports
s: Undervaluation is the target. Mexico's National Customs Agency (ANAM) demonstrated its Value Intelligence Platform, built to flag imports that may be declared below their real value, at the CONECTAA 2026 customs brokers' meeting, reported October 23. Sessions there, including a workshop with Google, covered AI for tariff classification, catching errors in customs declarations and predicting risk. Mexico Business News notes that automated flags don't prove wrongdoing on their own; people still review them.

h: Walmart lets customers' AI agents shop for them, with spending limits and rules
s: $50, $100 or $200: those are the example spending limits Walmart gave on October 21 for AI agents that will shop on a customer's behalf. Walmart announced three pieces. Agent Profiles, launching within the next month, give each authorized agent its own profile inside a customer's account, so its purchases show up separately; customers either approve every order or set a limit. The Walmart Agent Gateway, an invitation-only beta for agent builders, lets AI assistants connect directly to Walmart and Sam's Club systems to search and buy, Reuters reported. And new terms say agents need approval by default, never see payment card details, and get blocked if they break the rules. The Verge notes the contrast with Amazon, which has blocked outside shopping agents. Why it matters: an agent buying "the usual" picks from what product listings and stock data tell it, and launch lands right before holiday peak. Wrong pack sizes or stale availability can now cost an order without a human ever seeing the shelf.

h: Robots sorting Zalando returns now get tested fixes in days, not weeks
s: Days instead of weeks. That's how fast Sereact, NVIDIA, Nebius, CEVA Logistics and Zalando say a robot mistake on the returns line can now come back as a tested fix, under a training setup they announced on October 21. Recordings from the returns stations are turned into thousands of simulated variations, used to retrain Sereact's Cortex robot software, and scored against a pass mark before any update goes back to the floor. The first use is Zalando returns at CEVA sites, where Sereact's dual-arm stations went live in Greven, Germany and Świebodzin, Poland on October 7. The speed figure is the companies' own.

h: Opply raises $7.5M for AI agents that place and pay purchase orders
s: 15 times the gross revenue in 12 months. That's the growth Opply reported on October 21 as it raised $7.5 million in a round led by Chalfen Ventures. The London company's agents find suppliers, place and track purchase orders, check compliance documents and pay suppliers for food and drink brands, which repay Opply within 90 days, Tech Funding News reported. Opply cites customer cost cuts of 40%; Tech Funding News points out that part of that benefit comes from longer payment terms Opply extends, not only from better prices.

h: NVIDIA's DSX POD ships AI data centers as factory-built containers
s: Six months down to as little as 14 days. That's NVIDIA's estimate for bringing AI computing online at a prepared site with DSX POD, a design it introduced on October 21 in which partners build complete data-center modules inside containers. Each holds seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks plus networking, cabling and liquid cooling, all tested before shipping, Data Center Knowledge reported. NVIDIA names 17 partners, including Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Schneider Electric and Vertiv, with deliveries from early 2027. NVIDIA's own FAQ is clear that sites still need power, cooling water and network hookups ready first.

h: Treasury proposes new rules on US investment in foreign AI and chip companies
s: Comments are due December 7. The US Treasury proposed rules on October 22 under a 2025 law, the COINS Act, that would make US persons notify Treasury of certain investments in companies from countries of concern working on semiconductors, AI, quantum, supercomputing or hypersonics, and ban others outright. Treasury also proposed adding biotechnology. AP reports the targets include China, Russia and North Korea. The rules are a draft and can change before they're final.

h: Siemens puts an AI agent to work on production planning at its Erlangen plant
s: Up to 20% lower costs from an AI agent that drafts production plans: that's Siemens' own estimate from its electronics factory in Erlangen, Germany, where it showed new tools built with NVIDIA on October 19. When a new order arrives, the agent generates several production scenarios, shows planners how each one scores on defined KPIs, and checks the proposals against a digital twin of the whole plant before anything changes on the floor. A second tool trains the plant's inspection cameras on AI-generated images of new circuit boards, so quality checks can be set up before the first prototype exists; Siemens says that cuts engineering effort by up to 85% and time to market by up to 40%. German tech site Dr. Web notes these are best-case figures from Siemens and haven't been independently checked. Why it matters: a planning agent can only rank options against goals someone has written down, such as on-time delivery, changeovers, overtime and material shortages. Plants that haven't agreed on those will get fast answers to the wrong question.

h: Micron's Taiwan union plans a Thursday strike at an AI memory hub
s: A strike set for Thursday, October 22, at Micron's plant in Taoyuan, Taiwan, where the company makes DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI servers. The Taoyuan union announced it on October 19 to back a second union in a bonus dispute, timing it to that union's mediation meeting with Micron the same day, Reuters reported. The union hasn't said how long the walkout will last, and TrendForce says any hit to output depends on its size, its length and Micron's contingency plans.

h: Motive's new AI agents call truck drivers and open work orders on their own
s: It calls the driver itself. Motive launched Agents on October 19: AI that watches the safety and operations data on its fleet platform and acts, calling drivers in the cab through its Atlas assistant when it spots fatigue or bad weather ahead, opening a maintenance work order and marking a truck out of service when a fault code meets the fleet's rules, and prompting drivers to cut idling. Fleets choose the triggers and actions. Agents are available now to Motive customers, plain-language goals are promised for early next year, and Motive hasn't published results from fleets using it.

h: BMW's procurement agent answers capacity questions in minutes, and its language model does no math
s: Weeks down to a few minutes: that's how long BMW says it now takes to answer a question like "can we build more iX3s?" with its procurement agent, Mr. Flexibility, which it showed to journalists, automotiveIT reported on October 12. The agent pulls together the production program, agreed supplier capacity and engineering data, including battery-cell capacity at 13 supplier sites. The design is the lesson: the language model "calculates nothing," product owner Maik Leuthold told automotiveIT. Tested, rule-based tools do the math, each user sees only what they're allowed to see, stale data gets flagged, and people make the call. The weeks-to-minutes figure is BMW's own.

h: Free AI forecasting models just beat a classic method on grocery data
s: 4.5% to 6.3% less forecast error, with no training on the data. That's what Superlinear found when it tested Mistral's new Timestral models and Google's TimesFM against ETS, a classic statistical method many planning systems still rely on, using Walmart M5 food sales and a fresh-food dataset. Mistral released Timestral on October 15: four open-weight time-series models, from 5 million to 209 million parameters, that produce probabilistic forecasts, accept known future inputs such as planned promotions, and run on an ordinary CPU. In Superlinear's test, the small 28M version came within 0.4% of the largest model's accuracy in about a fifth of the time. Two cautions: Superlinear says Timestral is free only for companies under $20 million in monthly revenue, and it advises judging a forecast on service level, waste and stock, not error alone.

h: Microsoft walks away from the UK's biggest planned AI data center over power
s: No grid power until the 2030s: that's what Nscale was told about its planned data center in Loughton, Essex, which was meant to house about 23,000 Nvidia chips and open next year. Microsoft, its only publicly announced customer for the site, has ended its agreement, the BBC and the Guardian reported on October 18; Microsoft declined to comment. Nscale says it remains committed, is exploring alternative power sources, and that its Microsoft projects in Norway, Portugal and the US are unaffected.

h: An AI operator is auditing every LTL invoice at one freight broker
s: Nearly 3,500 audit decisions in two months, at 97% accuracy by the vendor's own count. That's what startup Evos reports for the AI operator that freight brokerage MyFreightWorld uses to check every LTL carrier invoice against its TMS; Evos says it closed out more than $600,000 of invoice value in the last five weeks. Evos came out of stealth on October 14 with $9 million in pre-seed funding, and it hasn't disclosed pricing or how much money the audits actually recovered.

h: China drafts export controls on AI and solar manufacturing technology
s: 40 technologies, 23 of them in AI. On October 16, China's commerce and science ministries published a draft adding large models, AI agents and computing clusters, plus 12 solar manufacturing technologies covering polysilicon, wafers, cells and the key equipment that carries them, to the country's restricted-export technology list. Comments run until November 15, but registration starts now: transferring or licensing listed technology abroad, or shifting its ownership or control to a foreign entity, must be registered first. Technology already open-sourced or published is excluded.

h: Robots are learning to pick shoeboxes at an s.Oliver warehouse
s: Shoeboxes have been close to impossible for general-purpose picking robots, according to Nomagic, and s.Oliver Group now plans to put the startup's Shoebox Picker to work. The fashion group selected Nomagic on October 14 to automate induction of a wide range of items, shoeboxes included, at its logistics site in Dettelbach, Germany, using AI vision and flexible robot handling. Neither company has given a go-live date, robot count or pick rates.

h: AI's appetite for memory just caused the worst quarter on record for smartphones
s: IDC's preliminary numbers show global smartphone shipments fell 22% year over year in the third quarter to about 255 million units, the steepest quarterly drop it has ever recorded. IDC blames the AI-driven memory shortage: memory costs are up roughly 350% from a year ago, and vendors have cut low-end models and raised prices. IDC expects pressure to last through 2027 and warns that some makers built ahead of next year's expected component squeeze, which could leave excess inventory if demand stays soft.

h: Taiwan plans to make unauthorized AI chip shipments to China a crime
s: Taiwan's economics minister, Kung Ming-hsin, told Bloomberg that Taipei will add AI servers and leading-edge semiconductors to its list of controlled goods, in line with commitments under its trade agreement with the US. Once the change takes effect, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization would become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act. Today, Taiwan can only pursue suspected smugglers under other laws. No start date has been given.

h: Adani and Jabil sign up to build AI racks and servers in India
s: Adani Enterprises and contract manufacturer Jabil signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding on October 13 for a 50:50 joint venture to make and assemble AI racks, servers, storage, networking gear, power distribution, liquid cooling and transformers in India, plus installation and commissioning. The companies are aiming for multi-gigawatt rack capacity for Indian and export customers. No investment figure or production date was given, and the deal still needs definitive agreements and approvals.

h: Kodiak's autonomous trucks now run reefer and dry freight to Laredo
s: Kodiak AI and carrier Charger Logistics are hauling refrigerated and dry-van freight for food, beverage and consumer-goods shippers on the 435-mile lane between Dallas and Laredo, the busiest US land port of entry. The first load ran September 8, and a safety driver is still on board until Kodiak finishes its safety case. Charger owns the trucks and runs Kodiak's driving system under a driver-as-a-service model, and it has a separate autonomy deal with Aurora on the same lane.

h: Robots are sorting Zalando's fashion returns without item-by-item training
s: Sereact's two-armed robots are now sorting Zalando returns in live operations at CEVA Logistics sites in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland. Sereact says its Cortex software lets the robots pick, identify and sort crumpled items they've never seen, without per-product setup or a fixed item list. The system is sold as robotics-as-a-service, and staff move to supervising stations, handling exceptions and checking quality. The companies call it the first step toward automating returns across Europe.

h: Amazon keeps blocking outside AI shopping agents, and now Grok Bot hits the wall
s: On October 15, users posted screenshots showing xAI's Grok Bot being stopped from ordering on Amazon with a notice that access by an unauthorized AI agent breaks Amazon's Conditions of Use. Elon Musk replied that users could buy elsewhere and floated starting an Amazon competitor, without giving details. Amazon hasn't publicly commented on Grok Bot, but it confirmed last month that it blocked Meta's Muse agent and is fighting Perplexity in court, arguing that agents should identify themselves and get the store's agreement.

h: TSMC: AI chip demand is still bigger than its capacity, and it's scouting Texas
s: TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of about $46.7B, up roughly 51% from a year ago, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3B to $54.3B. Management said AI-related demand remains very strong and the gap between demand and supply is still large, with 2026 capital spending planned at $60B to $64B. The WSJ reported that TSMC has sent teams to Texas to evaluate expansion beyond Arizona.

h: A Texas carrier adds Waabi's autonomous trucks to haul repeat freight
s: Warrior Logistics, an asset-based carrier with 200+ trucks, is running recurring food, beverage and consumer-goods loads on Waabi Driver-powered trucks between Dallas and Houston. Waabi says those routes have so far delivered 100% on-time pickup and delivery with no safety incidents, though neither company shared truck or load counts. Waabi also says its load volume on the lane is up more than 80% this year.

h: Ultra raises $50M to lease packing robots to warehouses by the month
s: Brooklyn-based Ultra closed a $50M Series A led by Framework Ventures, bringing total funding to $62M. It installs its OP1 packing robots at warehouses and third-party logistics sites for an upfront integration fee plus a monthly service fee, rather than a big capital purchase. The company says its robots have packed over 500,000 orders, and it relies on Physical Intelligence for the AI models that run them.

h: Kao's AI agent drafts demand plans, and people still make the call
s: In an English release this week, Japanese consumer-goods maker Kao detailed Kao-MIKOMIL, an AI agent that layers planned promotions, channels and pricing on top of forecasts from its in-house AI forecasting model, then proposes a demand plan with its reasoning. Business staff review and approve the plan. It went live for the KATE cosmetics brand in July and will expand to other brands, as part of Kao's goal to cut cosmetics inventory about 25% by 2027 versus 2024.

h: Samsara opens its no-code AI agent builder to all fleet customers
s: Samsara made Agent Studio generally available on October 13. Fleets can build chat and voice agents on their own operating data, for example to compile reports, flag possible hours-of-service violations, or answer driver questions from company policy. Samsara says agent use is now running at about seven times its June launch pace, but it hasn't said how many customers run agents in production.

h: Physical Intelligence opens its robot models to outside developers
s: Physical Intelligence launched a waitlisted beta of its Pi API on October 13. Teams upload their own robot data, fine-tune the company's general-purpose models on its managed infrastructure, and run them through a hosted service. Robots-as-a-service provider Formic, which says 150 factories use its robots, is an early partner. The company noted that network connectivity was a challenge in some early cloud-run deployments.

h: Scimplify raises $25M to add US capacity for specialty and critical-materials chemistry
s: Scimplify, a Bengaluru-based specialty chemicals and advanced materials maker, raised $25M in a round led by Hitachi Ventures, with Henkel and Teknor Apex joining. Total funding is now about $80M. It plans US research and processing capacity for areas with thin domestic supply, such as rare-earth and critical-metal purification and high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals, and will keep building its in-house AI platform for taking chemistry from lab to production.

h: Chip tariffs: the data-center exemption is still in limbo
s: January's Section 232 tariff put 25% on certain advanced logic chips but exempted chips headed for US data centers, pending a Commerce Department review that hasn't been published. On October 2, five tech trade groups including CCIA and TechNet asked the White House to keep any further chip, robotics and machinery tariffs targeted, and to extend any tariff offset program to downstream buyers. No second-phase decision has been announced.

h: Lumentum says its AI optics are sold out until about 2029
s: The CEO of optical-components maker Lumentum told Bloomberg the company is fully booked into early 2029. For some product lines, it can't fill about 70% of demand through 2027, and some customers are already placing orders for 2030. Six months ago, he expected to sell out only through 2028.

h: Adani and Jabil plan a 50:50 AI hardware joint venture in India
s: Adani Enterprises and contract manufacturer Jabil signed a non-binding MoU to build and assemble AI racks, servers, storage, networking, power and liquid-cooling gear in India at multi-gigawatt scale. The deal still needs definitive agreements and approvals, and no timeline has been announced.

h: GPU rental prices keep rising even as AI token prices fall
s: Posts on X highlighted that rental prices for top-end Nvidia GPUs climbed after per-token AI prices peaked, a classic Jevons effect: cheaper AI drives more usage. Silicon Data's B300 rental index launched near $6.95/GPU-hour, up roughly 44% since April. A separate marketplace tracker showed another weekly gain in early October.

h: Broadcom is lining up $30–50B+ to finance OpenAI's custom chips
s: The WSJ reported that Broadcom is working to arrange more than $50B in financing for the custom AI chips it is co-developing with OpenAI, with Apollo and Blackstone in talks. Bloomberg put the figure nearer $30B and called the talks early. Either way, private credit is now funding chip supply directly.

h: Shopify lets AI agents shop and check out, with spending limits
s: Shopify's Shop skill and Shop MCP let personal AI agents search a catalog of over 1 billion products, build carts and complete Shop Pay checkout. Shoppers approve purchases, or can set budgets that let the agent pay without asking. Shopify also reported its ecosystem supported 9.6M+ jobs in the year to June 2026.

h: TikTok tests an AI shopping assistant and one-click Buy Direct
s: TikTok is rolling out a conversational shopping assistant and Buy Direct, an in-feed checkout, to eligible advertisers. Integrations include Salesforce, Shopify and Stripe.

h: Practitioner tip: "boring AI" is the procurement win
s: A procurement practitioner described the most useful AI agent job in a single line: read supplier offers, compare them with your requirements, and flag what's missing. It's a narrow, checkable task, as opposed to an autonomous buyer.
